newsitem.title: USA: Dollar/mark surges on signs of strong U.S. economy. [CORRECTED 09:21 02/8]
newsitem.headline: Dollar/mark surges on signs of strong U.S. economy. [CORRECTED 09:21 02/8]

text.p: The dollar surged to a near eight-year high against the German mark on Friday, as fresh signs of strength in the U.S. job markets and manufacturing sector revived expectations of rising interest rates.
The dollar's rise, which came despite a sharp sell-off in the stock and bond markets, was also fuelled by concern about Europe's sluggish economy and uncertainty about the planned single currency.

The dollar was first buoyed by a surprisingly strong U.S. employment picture as American companies added 316,000 jobs to their payrolls in July, pushing the unemployment rate down 0.2 percent to 4.8 percent. This matched the level recorded in May, the lowest in nearly a quarter century.

"Dollar/mark (corrects from Dollar/yen) is going back to levels not seen since 1989," said Scott Siller, senior currency analyst at MCM CurrencyWatch. "We don't have any sign yet of when that dollar/mark rally is going to stop."
The dollar reached a high of 1.8665 marks Friday, a level not seen since November 1989.
The yen benefitted from the mark's weakness and the dollar ended little changed against the Japanese currency.
In late trading, the dollar was quoted at 1.8628 marks, up from 1.8385 late Thursday, and at 118.39 yen, vs. 118.65 yen.
Another boost for the dollar came from the National Association of Purchasing Management whose index of manufacturing activity rose to 58.6 in July from 55.7 in June.
The report also contained a hint of inflation as the index measuring the prices that manufacturers paid to their suppliers surged to 53.66 from 48.1.

Mike Malpede, senior analyst at Refco Group Ltd., said fears that the Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, had lost its resolve to defend the mark, in part, explained the dollar's impressive rally. Meanwhile, fears that Japanese officials would act to defend their currency prevented the dollar from scoring sharp gains against the yen, he said.
"I think there is greater fear of the Bank of Japan than of the Bundesbank. This has forced a lot of demand for the yen against the deutschemark," Malpede said.

John Hazelton, chief dealer at Manufacturers and Traders Bank, said the dollar has not surged against the yen due to market fears that U.S. and Japanese officials favour an exchange rate no higher than 120 yen.
"There are so many conflicting things going on with Japan," said Hazelton, referring to complex lingering trade tensions between the two nations.

The other winner of the day was sterling which gained more than two pfennigs to end at 3.04 marks as outgoing Bank of England Deputy Governor Howard Davies said the British economy may need somewhat higher interest rates.
The pound was quoted at $1.6305 late on Friday compared with $1.6403 on Thursday.
The dollar was higher at 1.5265 Swiss francs from Thursday's late quote at 1.5120 and at Canadian $1.3812 from C$1.3784.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury lost more than two points while its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, rose to 6.46 percent from 6.30 percent Thursday.
The Dow Jones industrial average suffered up to triple-digit losses but managed to end the day down 28.57 points at 8,194.04.
